name: Marco Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Marco. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent: no links to tech companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Anything you say is confidential. Can you tell me what a normal working day looks like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a company of about sixty people that makes billing software for local water boards and a few small energy co-ops. My corner is the invoice module, the part that turns meter readings into the bills people get in the post. It's old code, older than me in places, and most days I'm tracing why a customer in some village got charged twice for March.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's real. If I get it wrong, an old lady gets a wrong water bill, so I'm careful, and I like being careful. What wears me out is that I'm slow, and I know it. Kofi, who trained me, retires in three years and everyone keeps saying I'll take over the invoice code, which makes me proud and nervous at the same time.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No. The company doesn't allow it on customer data anyway, and I'm fine with that. I tried one once at home and it made up a function that doesn't exist, very confidently. I'd rather read the manual. My girlfriend Ana laughs at me, she says I'm twenty-seven going on sixty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: both sides oversold it. The people saying AI fixes everything and the people saying it ends everything were both selling something. Water still needs billing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means my plan still works. Learn the invoice code, take over from Kofi, get a pay rise when he goes. But the plan is slow, and I'm on low pay with about a fortnight of money in the bank, so slow is hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now, really. Keep learning the old code from Kofi, and write down everything he knows before he retires, because nobody else will. I'd ask about a small raise at my review in March. Ana and I would keep cooking at home and skip the holiday again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. Not because of AI. Because there's only one other software firm in our town and I'm not good enough yet to get hired there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if something went wrong with money before Kofi retires?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd be stuck quickly. Ana works early shifts at the bakery on the market square, and her pay is less than mine. One broken boiler and we'd be on her parents' sofa, and they live an hour away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're proud and nervous about taking over. Which is bigger?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, today. Kofi carries twenty years of why things are the way they are in his head. If I don't get that out of him in three years, I'm the guy holding code nobody understands, me included.

say: **Both sides** oversold AI; the boosters and the doomers were both **selling something**.
Water still needs **billing**, and that hasn't changed.
think: My plan still works: **take over** the invoice code when Kofi retires.
The plan is **slow**, and slow is hard on low pay with **a fortnight** saved.
do: Write down **everything Kofi knows** about the invoice code before he retires.
Ask for a **small raise** at the March review.
Keep **cooking at home** and skip the holiday again with Ana.
feel: **Uneasy**, mainly because he isn't good enough yet for the town's **only other** software firm.
S0.quote: The people saying AI fixes everything and the people saying it ends everything were both selling something.
fieldNote: Marco's security rests on **one person**: his trainer Kofi, retiring in three years.
His worry is **thin savings** and few local jobs, not AI.
He likes the company's **AI ban** and sees caution as part of his job.

steps.text: Write a handbook of Kofi's knowledge about the invoice module
Ask for a small raise at the March review
Skip the summer holiday and cook at home with Ana

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's be sensible: test it on the boring stuff first, keep it away from customer bills until it's proven. I'm not against it, I'm against rushing. I'd say that in the team meeting, politely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the company would use it to replace me before Kofi even retires. If a tool can read old billing code and explain it, then the thing that makes me worth keeping, knowing that code, isn't rare anymore. And I've never touched these tools, so I'd be behind the people who have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to start using it, even though I don't want to. I'd ask our team lead, Greta, if there's training, and do it on work time, not at home. I'd also look at the jobs board for the council's IT department, because councils move slowly and that suits me. And I'd stop putting money into the gym and the phone upgrade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, properly. Being patient with old code is the thing I'm good at, and it might stop counting for anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn it even though you don't want to. What's stopping you from wanting to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like learning to use the thing that takes your seat. And I don't trust it with bills. If it gets one rule wrong, ten thousand people get the wrong bill, and it's my name on the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The two testers, Lukas and Abby. Checking is right there on that list you read. They're good people and they've both got young kids, which I don't. If it came down to it, I'd almost rather it was me.

say: Test AI on **boring tasks** first and keep it away from **customer bills** until proven.
I'm not against AI; I'm against **rushing** it.
think: If a tool can explain old billing code, my **rare knowledge** isn't rare anymore.
I've never used these tools, so I'd be **behind** the people who have.
do: Ask Greta for **AI training** on work time, not at home.
Check the **council IT** jobs board, since councils move slowly.
Cancel the **gym** and the phone upgrade.
feel: **Properly worried** that patience with old code might stop **counting** for anything.
S1.quote: Being patient with old code is the thing I'm good at, and it might stop counting for anything.
fieldNote: Marco's reluctance is about **trust and blame**: his name on a wrong bill.
He'd learn AI **under protest**, and only on work time.
He'd almost sacrifice his own job for **testers with kids**, which shows his values.

steps.text: Ask Greta for AI training on work time
Check the council IT jobs board every week
Cancel the gym membership and the phone upgrade

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what I'd say. Probably nothing clever. I'd say someone needs to slow this down, and I'd mean the government, but I'm not a protest person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be finished and I wouldn't know what to do about it. My whole job is reading and changing code at a screen, and the robots coming in 2031 doesn't help someone like me. Two years isn't enough to learn anything new well, not at my speed, and we've got no money to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I really don't have a plan. I'd keep going to work every day because what else, and hope the water boards are slow to switch, which they might be. I'd ask Ana's uncle, who has a building firm, if he'd take me on as a labourer, because at least that lasts until the robots. Beyond that I'd be leaning on Ana's family, and I hate saying that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked, if I'm honest. Like the floor's gone and I'm just standing there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maybe the water boards are slow to switch. How much do you believe that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little. They still send some bills on paper, so they're not quick. But if AGI is cheaper than all of us, even a slow customer switches eventually, and two years isn't eventually, it's next week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Ana talk about that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether to give up the flat and move in with her parents. Whether to put off getting married, which we'd half planned for next year. I think she'd be braver about it than me; she gets up at four for the bakery, she's tougher.

say: Someone, meaning the **government**, needs to **slow this down**.
I'm **not a protest person**, so I'd mostly say nothing clever.
think: My job is all **screen work**, so robots in 2031 don't help me.
Two years isn't enough to **learn something new** at my speed, with no money.
do: Keep going to work and **hope** the water boards are slow to switch.
Ask **Ana's uncle** about labouring work at his building firm.
Consider **moving in** with Ana's parents and putting off the **wedding**.
feel: **Panicked**, like the floor has gone and he's just standing there.
S2.quote: If AGI is cheaper than all of us, even a slow customer switches eventually, and two years isn't eventually, it's next week.
fieldNote: Marco has **no plan**, no savings and little appetite for change; that's what panic looks like.
His only shelter idea is **labouring** until robots arrive in 2031.
He sees his partner as **tougher** and expects to lean on her family.

steps.text: Keep maintaining the invoice code and hope the water boards switch slowly
Ask Ana's uncle for labouring work at his building firm
Move in with Ana's parents to save the rent
Postpone the wedding planned for next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as with the slow change: be careful, test things, don't rush. Maybe I'd add that companies should tell staff early what they're planning. That's fair and doesn't take sides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better, but it still ends my job, just in 2031. I'd have time to get Kofi's knowledge into my head and maybe get his job before it goes. That's a strange thing to aim for, a promotion into something that disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay and keep learning the invoice code, and I'd finally learn the AI tools, slowly, maybe from 2027. I'd look into a part-time course in something with my hands, maybe plumbing, which Ana's uncle says always needs people. That gives me until about 2034, which is a few more years. And we'd try hard to save, even fifty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Less frozen than with two years, but still not sleeping great. I'm not someone who changes quickly, and five years is quick for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why plumbing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ana's uncle says every house he builds needs a plumber and he can never get one. Fixing pipes is fixing things that are broken, which is what I do now, just with water instead of bills. Funny, actually: still water.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the AI tools 'slowly, maybe from 2027'. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't believe it until I see it, and in 2027 I'd see more. I know that sounds like an excuse. It probably is.

say: Be **careful** with AI and test things on the boring work first; don't rush.
Companies should **tell staff early** what they're planning, which is fair and doesn't take sides.
think: Five years still **ends my job**, just in 2031.
Aiming to take over **Kofi's job** means a promotion into something that **disappears**.
do: Keep learning the **invoice code** and start AI tools slowly from **2027**.
Look into a **part-time plumbing** course through Ana's uncle's contacts.
Try to save even **fifty a month**.
feel: **Alarmed** and not sleeping well, because five years is **quick** for him.
S3.quote: Fixing pipes is fixing things that are broken, which is what I do now, just with water instead of bills.
fieldNote: Marco sees **plumbing** as a natural cousin of fixing billing errors.
He openly calls his delay on AI tools **an excuse**.
He expects to lose his job and lacks savings, so he stays **alarmed** despite five years.

steps.text: Learn the invoice code from Kofi before he retires
Start a part-time plumbing course through Ana's uncle's contacts
Put fifty a month into a savings account
Wait until 2027 before learning the AI coding tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do it properly, and I'd say that to anyone. No rushing, no panic. Plan it like a big billing migration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably take over from Kofi, do that for a few years, and be in my mid-thirties when it lands. That's enough time to save something and train in a trade. I'm slow, but ten years is slow enough even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First few years, nothing different: learn the invoice code, take Kofi's job in 2029 when he retires. I'd learn the AI tools once everyone else has, which would be by then anyway. Around 2032 I'd start a plumbing apprenticeship in the evenings, so I'm qualified before 2036, with robots not until 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but it's a normal anxious, the kind I've always had about money. Not the floor-falling kind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does ten years change for you and Ana?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd get married next year like we planned, and maybe think about a child around thirty. With two years, none of that. With ten, life goes on, just with a plan in the drawer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that still bothers you in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money. Ten years of low pay and nothing saved is still ten years of one broken boiler away from trouble. AI or not, that's the bit that bothers me.

say: Ten years is enough time to do it **properly**, with no rushing.
Plan it like a big **billing migration**.
think: I'd take over from **Kofi** and be in my mid-thirties when AGI lands.
I'm slow, but **ten years** is slow enough even for me.
do: Take **Kofi's job** when he retires in 2029.
Learn the AI tools **once everyone else** has.
feel: A **normal anxious** about money, not the floor-falling kind.
S4.quote: Ten years of low pay and nothing saved is still ten years of one broken boiler away from trouble.
fieldNote: With ten years Marco's **life plans** go ahead: wedding next year, maybe a child.
His mood stays **anxious** because the money problem exists **without AI**.
He uses his own trade's language: plan it like a **migration**.

steps.text: Take over the invoice module when Kofi retires in 2029
Start an evening plumbing apprenticeship around 2032
Go ahead with the wedding to Ana next year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd have no plan and no money, and I don't move fast. What would help is someone telling me plainly which jobs are safe for the next few years, and paid training for those, because I can't afford to guess wrong.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who checks the AI's work on things like bills. Somebody has to answer when a pensioner gets charged twice. A computer can't say sorry on the phone to someone's gran.

headlineQuote: A computer can't say sorry on the phone to someone's gran.
portrait: Marco, 27, maintains the **invoice module** of billing software used by local water boards and energy co-ops.
He **never uses AI**, likes his firm's ban, and is learning old code from Kofi, who retires in three years.
He lives with his girlfriend Ana, a bakery worker, with about **a fortnight** of savings and few local jobs.
Fast AGI leaves him **panicked** with no plan; with more time he plans a move into **plumbing**.
He's pragmatic and blames **no one side**, but his low pay worries him in every scenario.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd have no plan, no money and doesn't move fast.
whatWouldHelp: Plain advice on **which jobs** stay safe, and **paid training** for them.
